# Mexico kick off World Cup with 2-0 win over South Africa amid three red cards

Mexico's misery in World Cup opening games was finally ended as they secured a 2-0 win over South Africa at the Estadio Azteca in a match featuring three red cards.

The co-hosts had been involved in seven matches which either alone, or jointly, opened previous tournaments, but had won none of them.

They put that right at the eighth attempt however as goals from Julián Quiñones and Fulham's Raúl Jiménez in either half gave them a victorious start against a South Africa side who finished with nine men.

Cesar Montes' dismissal in stoppage time took some of the shine off an otherwise upbeat afternoon. [...] South Africa substitute Themba Zwane was sent off after a VAR review for appearing to strike Alvarado in the face late on as the pair tangled, on a day which firmly belonged to the host nation. Brazilian referee Wilton Sampaio produced one more red, sending off Montes in stoppage time for a challenge on Khuliso Mudau.

content:
In what was a captivating start to the FIFA World Cup, Mexico secured a 2-0 victory over South Africa, marking a significant moment as they ended a streak of disappointing opening matches in World Cup history. The win, achieved in front of a vibrant home crowd at Mexico City Stadium, featured early brilliance from Julián Quiñones, who scored the opener just nine minutes into the match, and a second goal from Raúl Jiménez in the 67th minute, solidifying Mexico's position as the Group A leaders.

What stood out in this match was not just the scoreline but the intense drama that unfolded, highlighted by three red cards. Ronwen Williams, South Africa's goalkeeper, noted the harsh lessons learned in this match, emphasizing the need for discipline and the importance of capitalizing on opportunities at this elite level. The South African side, despite being outplayed, showed resilience, with Williams stating, “We’ll keep fighting, we’ll keep going as a team, and we’ll be better” (Source 1).

From a tactical perspective, Mexico's approach was aggressive from the outset, with Erik Lira's interception leading to Quinones' goal, reflecting a proactive mindset. Despite dominating possession and chances, Mexico's late-game discipline faltered with the sending off of Cesar Montes for a challenge that took some gloss off the victory (Source 2). 

The match also had historical resonance, as this was Mexico's first victory in an opening World Cup game after seven previous attempts without a win, a fact that adds a layer of psychological relief for the co-hosts (Source 2). 

Overall, while Mexico's performance was commendable, the three red cards serve as a reminder of the need for composure, particularly as the tournament progresses. The victory not only boosts their confidence but sets the tone for their campaign in a group that also includes competitive teams like South Korea and Czechia. As the tournament unfolds, fans and analysts alike will be keen to see how Mexico builds on this crucial win.

content:
In a thrilling opening match of the FIFA World Cup, Mexico emerged victorious over South Africa with a 2-0 scoreline, marking a historic moment as they finally secured a win in their eighth attempt at starting a World Cup tournament (Source 2). Goals from Julián Quiñones and Raúl Jiménez not only set the tone for Mexico's campaign but also showcased their attacking prowess in front of a fervent home crowd at the Mexico City Stadium.

The match was laden with drama, highlighted by a total of three red cards—two for South Africa and one for Mexico's César Montes—underscoring the intensity of the contest (Source 1, Source 2). South Africa's goalkeeper, Ronwen Williams, reflected on the harsh lessons learned, noting the importance of maintaining discipline and seizing opportunities at this level of competition. He expressed a commitment to improve, stating, “We’ll keep fighting, we’ll keep going as a team, and we’ll be better” (Source 1).

From a tactical standpoint, Mexico displayed an aggressive approach right from the kickoff. Quiñones' opening goal came just nine minutes into the match after Erik Lira capitalized on a mistake by South Africa's Sphephelo Sithole, driving a low shot past Williams (Source 2). This early strike not only deflated South Africa but also set the stage for a confident display by the hosts. Despite dominating possession and creating several chances—including a near second goal for Quiñones that hit the post—Mexico's final moments were marred by Montes' late dismissal, which could raise concerns about discipline as the tournament progresses (Source 2).

Overall, Mexico's performance was a blend of resilience and opportunity, marking a strong start in Group A as they currently sit atop the standings. While they must address the disciplinary issues highlighted by the red cards, the victory instills confidence and sets a positive trajectory for their upcoming matches against competitive teams like South Korea and Czechia. The opening win not only provides a psychological boost but also reinforces Mexico's status as a contender in this World Cup.
